extracted.intended_audience: information science researchers, scientometrics and science-communication scholars (and practitioners interested in what makes research newsworthy)
extracted.subtask_description: Building predictive models and identifying factors that determine whether a scholarly research article will receive news coverage; the paper uses altmetric features and classification models to operationalize 'newsworthiness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest / topical relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic is of interest to the public or the findings have a perceptible impact on society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science journalists present stories they think their readers are likely to find interesting; mentions by news outlets often establish the relevance the research has to society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excitement / fascination value
rubrics_metrics.description: Research is assessed as exciting or particularly relevant to readers (fascination value).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rensberger identified 'fascination value' as one of the factors that make science news; editors/journalists select stories judged to be exciting to their audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustworthiness / validity of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: The trustworthiness and validity of the research—how credible and reliable the findings are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With fact-checking journalism, audiences generally assume validity is confirmed prior to news presentation; earlier studies criticized inaccurate coverage, making trustworthiness a key factor in making science news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige of the journal
rubrics_metrics.description: The prestige or reputation of the journal in which the research is published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige is cited (along with prepublication publicity and relevance) as a factor that might impact whether research is considered newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepublication publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicity or promotion of findings before formal publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepublication publicity can influence selection for coverage; it's one of the factors discussed in prior work as affecting newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance to a specific audience
rubrics_metrics.description: How relevant the findings are to a given audience or readership segment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior work notes that relevance to a target audience is a determinant of selection for news coverage; journalists pick stories tailored to their readers' interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of impact / number of people affected
rubrics_metrics.description: The magnitude of impact measured by how many people are affected by the findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies referenced indicate that stories affecting larger numbers of people are more likely to be considered newsworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to adapt traditional news values for science
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional newsworthiness factors developed for politics/culture may be misleading for science and require adaptation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Badenschier and Wormer concluded that using conventional news-selection factors without adaptation can misrepresent what makes scientific issues newsworthy; a science-specific adaptation is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism / accuracy in coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: News coverage should avoid overstatement, sensationalism, and factual inaccuracies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Earlier critiques highlight inaccurate coverage, overstatement of results, and sensationalism as problems; implicitly, accurate and measured reporting supports legitimate newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online attention (altmetric activity) across platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Counts/mentions on social and online platforms (Twitter, Wikipedia, Google+, Weibo, Facebook, videos, blogs, peer reviews, Mendeley) as indicators of attention correlated with news coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study relied on mentions on Twitter, Wikipedia, Google+, Weibo, Facebook, videos, blogs, peer reviews, and Mendeley; Mendeley counts were most significant for the Random Forest model, Video was least significant for RF, and different classifiers gave different relative importances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature selection: remove sparse or irrelevant features
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclude features that are very sparse or no longer relevant (e.g., Pinterest, StackOverflow activity, policy citation counts, discontinued services like Connotea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors filtered out fields based on sparsity and lack of relevance; Connotea was removed because it was discontinued and irrelevant for later publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset labeling and balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Binary class label: articles with at least one news mention vs. articles with no news coverage; use balanced sampling to avoid class imbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors randomly selected 50,000 research articles from each category (news vs. no news) to produce a 100,000-article dataset without class imbalance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling approach: use multiple classifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Train and compare multiple classification algorithms (e.g., SVM with RBF kernel, Random Forest with 100 trees, Multinomial Naïve Bayes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparing several models helps identify best-performing approach; in this study Random Forest performed best (accuracy 0.924).

rubrics_metrics.name: Training/validation procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an 80/20 train/test split and 10-fold cross-validation when building models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors trained on 80% of data, tested on 20%, and used 10-fold CV; follow standard ML validation to estimate generalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation metrics for predictive performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Report accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, ROC curves and area under the ROC curve (AUC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper presents accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 for each model and shows ROC curves/AUC to compare classifiers comprehensively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature importance analysis and kernel limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute feature weights or importance to determine each feature's relative contribution; note that some models/kernels (e.g., SVM with RBF) do not allow straightforward feature weight calculation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors calculated weights for RF and MNB; SVM with RBF could not provide feature weights because weights are only directly computable for linear kernels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Future modeling extension: regression for counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond classification, build regression models to predict the number (count) of news mentions an article is likely to receive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors propose improving classification models and developing regression models as future work to predict count of mentions from news outlets.
